title: When a Big Customer Fires You, Sell Value Not Price
documentTitle: Google/Hearst: Written Response to Concerns — Email from Jonathan Bellack to Philip Wiser et al. (January 25, 2017)
excerptForBlog: I am head of product management for DFP and the DoubleClick Ad Exchange. I have been working closely with your account team here at Google on matters related to your upcoming renewal that have led to Hearst Magazines deactivating AdX as a demand source. I really value our partnership, so I want to extend our regrets that the relationship between our companies has reached the point that you saw turning off the Ad Exchange as your next step. All of us here at Google are committed to helping turn things around and proving to you that the Ad Exchange can continue to help you meet your goals in 2017 and beyond. To help rebuild trust, we have provided detailed, confidential responses on each Hearst concern in the attached PDF document. In summary, the key points are: 1 - we are offering our engineering and analytic resources to participate in a transparent and fair test, because we believe that by completely turning off AdX, you are losing out on unique demand from our ad network (GDN) and higher yields from our DSP (DBM); 2 - we are offering to discuss your broader ad technology cost structure, because we believe that there may be other opportunities for Google to reduce costs, beyond DFP & AdX fees; 3 - we are offering price concessions which we feel offer fair value for money, because we believe that selecting the low-cost vendor in ad tech is not a recipe for sustainable long-term growth.

lessonTitle: When a Big Customer Fires You, Sell Value Not Price
pullQuote: When a customer pulls the plug, you have one shot — show them what they're losing, not just what you'll discount.
leadershipTraits: reframes the debate instead of accepting the customer's frame
thinks about precedent, not just the deal in front of him
leads with structure — test, cost review, concessions
situation: In January 2017, Jonathan Bellack, Google's head of product for DFP and the DoubleClick Ad Exchange, emailed Philip Wiser and others at Hearst Magazines. Hearst had already pulled the trigger — they deactivated AdX as a demand source. Bellack is writing to prevent a full break before a contract renewal, with real ad revenue on the line for both sides.
insight: Bellack doesn't just apologize and ask for another chance. He structures three specific offers: an engineering-led transparent test, a broader cost review beyond DFP and AdX fees, and price concessions. Each offer is paired with a concrete reason — 'you are losing out on unique demand from our ad network' and 'higher yields from our DSP.' That pairing matters. He's not just offering carrots; he's making a business case that leaving costs Hearst money. The third point is the sharpest: he argues that 'selecting the low-cost vendor in ad tech is not a recipe for sustainable long-term growth.' He's reframing the conversation from price to total value — a classic move when a competitor is undercutting you on fees. The hidden move here is confidence: he offers the test because he believes Google will win it. That's not a concession; it's a trap door back to the relationship on Google's terms.
application: If a customer cancels or threatens to leave over price or trust, don't just discount. Propose a structured, time-bound test that lets your product prove its value on neutral ground. Make the business case for what they lose by switching — not what they gain by staying. That reframes you from vendor to partner, and puts the burden of proof on the exit, not the renewal.
